title: Slide 1 · Reading event histories
question: A plan said “check ID, then hand over C1.” The desk wants to know what actually happened on Ava’s request. What would you look for?
answer: Look for observations of each action tied to Ava’s request, with their event times. The plan alone gives the intended order.

title: Slide 2 · What happened to this request?
question: Could Ava’s name and the camera’s ID, together, replace the request ID in this example?
answer: No. Both requests would share exactly those values. The request ID lets us determine which check belongs with which handoff.

title: Slide 3 · Seeing two events is different from ordering them
question: R8 is marked False even though the log shows an ID check. What exactly failed?
answer: R8’s check at minute 7 came after its handoff at minute 4. The presence of the check alone cannot establish the required order.

title: Slide 4 · Leave room for an incomplete record
question: What additional evidence would help when both events show minute 6?
answer: A reliable within-minute sequence number or more precise event times for the same request could establish which action occurred first.

title: Slide 5 · Explain the result using the original records
question: A clerk says, “The check came after handoff because E12 was entered last.” What correction can you support?
answer: E12 records the check at minute 2, before the minute-5 handoff in E13. Its later entry at minute 8 describes when the record arrived. These records support the required event order.

title: Slide 6 · Compare event time with entry time
question: Replace this line: rows = [("E12", "check", 2, 8), ("E13", "handoff", 5, 5)] with: rows = [("E12", "check", 2, 8), ("E13", "handoff", 5, 9)] What will print?
answer:
E12 then E13
E12 then E13
Only the handoff’s entry time changed. With 8 before 9, the order of the entries now agrees with the event order.

title: Slide 8 · From this module to the next
question: The recorded wait fell just after an extra clerk arrived. What outcome is missing if you want to know whether the extra clerk caused the drop?
answer: You would need to know how the queue would have changed over the same period without extra help. The event order establishes which happened first and leaves that alternative outcome unobserved.

title: Office hours · Why bother with a process if a knowledge graph can store both actions?
question: Why bother with a process if a knowledge graph can store both actions?
answer: A graph can represent when an event happened and which request it concerns. Those details let you ask whether a particular check preceded a particular handoff. A graph containing only the broad facts “Ava was checked” and “C1 was handed over” cannot answer that question about R7.

title: Office hours · If I see the check first and the handoff second, did the check cause the handoff?
question: If I see the check first and the handoff second, did the check cause the handoff?
answer: The log supports a statement about sequence. To ask about a cause, imagine changing whether the check happened and ask what that change would do to the outcome. A log of one sequence observes only what actually happened.

title: Exercise 1
question: Request R11 has handoff H1 at 12, check C2 at 14 and an earlier check C1 at 9. The rule requires at least one earlier check. Does H1 pass?
answer: Yes. C1 at 9 is earlier than H1 at 12. C2 at 14 cannot support H1, but the rule only asks for one earlier check.

title: Exercise 2
question: A return and a new loan share a camera. Which columns would let someone audit the order of steps in each loan even if the logs arrive late?
answer: Keep a distinct loan ID, item ID, action, event time, entry time and evidence-row ID. Group by loan, order by event time and use row IDs to cite the evidence. Record clock precision or a reliable sequence number if times can tie.

title: Exercise 3
question: A dashboard counts 7 in order, 2 reversed and 1 missing. Of the 10 cases, what fraction has evidence of following the rule? Of the cases whose order is known, what fraction followed it?
answer: Seven of ten cases have supporting evidence. Among the nine with known order, seven of nine followed it. Report the missing case so readers know why the fractions differ.

title: Lab case 1 · Two visits
question: Does either request have evidence of a check before its own handoff?
answer: Neither does. R7 has no handoff record. R8 has no check record. Combining the visits would manufacture a completed sequence.

title: Lab case 2 · Whole-minute clock
question: Which status should the desk show, and why?
answer: Order unknown. The two entries establish that both actions were recorded during minute 10. They leave their order unresolved.

title: Lab case 3 · Late entry
question: Which clock answers whether the physical steps followed the rule?
answer: Use event times for the physical order. The recorded check at 11 preceded handoff at 15. Entry times 18 and 16 would reverse that order.

title: Module overview · Reading event histories
question: What is this module about?
answer: Reading event histories. Decide whether one request’s records support a required order of events, and explain how a missing or tied time limits the answer.
